newsitem.title: UK: UK prepares law on jailing foreign dissidents.
newsitem.headline: UK prepares law on jailing foreign dissidents.

text.p: Britain is preparing a law which would allow authorities to jail foreign dissidents who plotted against other countries, government sources said on Wednesday.

The sources confirmed a story in Thursday's Independent newspaper which said dissidents conspiring to overthrow foreign governments or to cause "substantive acts" abroad could face imprisonment if the new law was approved.

The paper said Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard was determined to close a legal loophole which allowed London-based Saudi dissident Mohammad al-Masari to mount a campaign calling for the overthrow of the Saudi royal family.
Howard tried to deport Masari but was over-ruled in April by an immigration appeals tribunal, which gave the fundamentalist Islamic dissident leave to stay in Britain for four years.
His campaign against the Saudi royal family strained relations with Britain and caused British businessmen to complain about losing lucrative contracts.

London is home to numerous exile groups and opposition newspapers from around the world but critics have attacked the government for not doing enough to stop an active minority from fomenting trouble abroad.
One of the reasons why Britain attracts exiled activists is that, under the present law, refugees do not have to stop political activities when claiming asylum.
Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin and Italian revolutionary Guiseppe Mazzini are just two of the foreign activists who have used London as a base.

The Independent said the anti-subversive legislation was being prepared one of eight draft laws to be proposed by parliamentarians whose names were drawn in a ballot to introduce private member's bills.
There is no guarantee that bills introduced in this way will reach the statute books.
The hijacking of a Sudanese airliner to London in August focused attention on whether Britain's liberal attitude towards political refugees had made it a haven for those planning violence abroad.
Saudi officials were infuriated by Masari's remarks supporting what he called the intellectual arguments behind a bomb attack in Dhahran in which 19 U.S. servicemen were killed.
Masari also wrote that the people of Palestine, Syria, Jordan, Egypt and Lebanon had a "specific obligation" to annihilate Jews because they had seen their lands occupied.
